sentences.text: Last time, you built a divide-by-five counter by giving its five states a plain binary count.
It worked, and its next-state logic cost three gates.
Two and gates, and an exclusive-or.
This time, the same five states get some funkier codes.
The lecturer calls them just a bit of fun, not something you'd necessarily do for real.
But they show how much freedom you have when you choose the codes.
Can a cleverer choice make the logic almost disappear?
And if it can, what do you pay for it instead?
These funkier assignments often borrow the action of a shift register.
In a shift register, every edge of the clock passes each flip-flop's value on to the next.
The first example is called the sliding assignment.
We start with all three flip-flops at zero, drawn in the table's order, with flip-flop A on the right.
On the first edge of the clock, a one enters flip-flop A.
On the next edge, it slides along to flip-flop bee, and a second one enters behind it.
On the third edge, both ones slide along together.
On the fourth, the first one drops off the far end.
On the fifth, the second one drops off too, and every flip-flop is back at zero.
So the five states get the codes zero zero zero, zero zero one, zero one one, one one zero, and one zero zero, and then round again.
Why send in two ones?
The output must be one in two of the five states, and we'd like to take it straight from a flip-flop.
A single one passing through would hold each flip-flop at one for just one state.
Two of them, one right behind the other, hold each flip-flop at one for two states in a row.
Check it on the columns.
Flip-flop A reads zero, one, one, zero, zero.
Flip-flop bee reads zero, zero, one, one, zero.
And flip-flop see reads three zeros, then two ones.
Each is high for two states and low for three, the waveform we want.
In fact they're the same waveform, each one period behind the last.
The specification never says where the output's cycle should start, so any of the three can be the output.
Here's the transition table for the sliding assignment.
Each state's next state is simply the code that follows it in the sequence.
Three patterns never occur: zero one zero, one zero one, and one one one.
Notice that zero one zero is unused here, though the binary count used it.
Which patterns are unused depends on the assignment.
Now plot a K-map for the input of flip-flop A, with the unused states as don't cares, just as in part one.
The next value of flip-flop A is one in just two states, zero zero zero and zero zero one.
They sit side by side, so they make a pair, and the input to flip-flop A is not bee and not see.
The don't cares can't make a bigger group, so we leave them out.
For the other two flip-flops, you don't even need a K-map.
Look at the column for flip-flop A in the current state.
It reads zero, one, one, zero, zero.
Now look at the column for flip-flop bee in the next state.
It's exactly the same.
So dee bee equals A, which is just a wire.
In the same way, the current column for bee matches the next column for see, so dee see equals bee.
As the lecturer puts it, we like things where we don't have to do anything.
Put the three together.
Flip-flop bee copies A, and flip-flop see copies bee, on every edge of the clock.
That's a shift register, running from A to bee to see.
The only logic is the and gate at its input, and you can read it in words.
A new one enters flip-flop A only when bee and see are both zero.
Here's the sliding counter as a circuit, laid out the way the lecturer drew it in his simulator.
As in part one, the circuit puts flip-flop A on the left, so here the ones slide to the right.
Just one gate is needed, an and gate.
It takes the not-bee and not-see outputs, and feeds flip-flop A.
Then the output of flip-flop A is wired straight into the input of flip-flop bee, and the output of bee into flip-flop see.
It starts with all three flip-flops at zero, which is the first state in our table.
On every edge of the clock, the ones slide one place along.
The lecturer takes the output from flip-flop bee, though any of them would do.
It's high for two periods of the clock, then low for three, again and again.
So the sliding assignment uses the same three flip-flops as the binary count, but one gate instead of three.
It needs less wiring too, because two of its three inputs are plain wires from a neighbour.
Can we go further, and get rid of that last gate?
Next comes the shift register assignment, what the lecturer calls an even more egregious use of flip-flops.
Take a shift register, and connect the output of its last flip-flop back to the input of its first.
Now whatever is inside just cycles round and round.
Use five flip-flops, from flip-flop A to flip-flop ee, and put two ones side by side in the ring.
They have to be neighbours, so that each output stays high for two states in a row.
On every edge of the clock, the pair moves one step round the ring.
In the table's order, with flip-flop A on the right, the first state is zero zero zero one one.
The next is zero zero one one zero.
The pair moves one place left each time, and wraps round from the left end back to the right.
After five steps, it's back where it started.
That's five flip-flops for five states, two more than the minimum of three.

The next column for flip-flop bee matches the current column for flip-flop A, so dee bee equals A.
The rest follow the same way.

That's no surprise, because it's exactly how the ring is wired.
Each flip-flop's input is the output of the flip-flop before it.
Laid out as a circuit, it's five flip-flops in a row, sharing one clock signal, with one long wire from the last back to the first.
There are no gates at all, only wires.
Five flip-flops can hold thirty-two patterns, and we use only five.

The lecturer calls these last two designs just a couple of bits of fun.
But they show that you can build a working machine with no combinational logic at all, from flip-flops alone.
And sometimes that's the cheaper design.
On a modern chip, each flip-flop takes up only a little room.
Logic gates need wiring between them, and wiring takes up space.
So using more flip-flops to avoid the logic can be the better choice.
Those were the slide's two points in part one, about area and wiring.

Sliding used three flip-flops and one gate.
